title: The art of conversation
hook: he loved a good, sharp conversation and hated flattery (Essays 3.8)

segments.voice: Yesterday, not too much: Montaigne warns we can grip even a virtue so hard it turns into a fault. Your line was not too much. Where did you stop one step earlier? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-one.

Somebody at the table says something you think is wrong. There are a few moves available. Nod and change the subject. Agree out loud and disagree in the car on the way home. Or say, wait, I don't think that's right, and see what happens. Montaigne knew which one he wanted, from himself and from whoever was talking with him. He wrote a whole essay about talking, and in it he says he'd rather be contradicted than flattered. Today, the art of conversation.
screen: `SOMEONE SAYS SOMETHING WRONG.` → `NOD, OR SAY IT?` → `CONTRADICT ME, PLEASE.`

segments.voice: First, how much he prized it. In the essay Of the art of conversing, Montaigne calls conversation the most fruitful and natural exercise of our minds. He finds it sweeter than any other act of life, he says, so much that he'd sooner give up his sight than his hearing or his speech. Second, what he wanted from it. Not agreement. When someone opposes him, he says, it wakes his attention, not his anger. He moves toward the person who contradicts him, because that person is teaching him. Truth is welcome from any hand, and he means to give it a cheerful welcome, even when it beats him. Third, what he couldn't stand. Talk where everyone defers and applauds bores him; he calls that kind of company soft. He wants a friendship strong enough to enjoy sharpness and vigor in the way people talk. Flattery, to him, wastes the whole point. If the other person only agrees, nothing gets tested. Fourth, the hard part. Much of the essay is about how talk goes wrong: people get heated, stubborn, more attached to winning than to finding out. Montaigne's art isn't about being clever. It's about caring more for the truth than for your own side of the table. At the next dinner table, that might be one sentence: I see it differently, and here's why. Then listening to the answer.
screen: `THE MIND'S MOST FRUITFUL EXERCISE.` · `CONTRADICTION WAKES HIS ATTENTION.` · `FLATTERY WASTES THE POINT.` · `TRUTH OVER WINNING.` · then, large: `HONEST TALK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready for one honest conversation. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you'll talk to today or soon. Is there one thing you've been nodding along to that you see differently? Find the plain, kind sentence that says so. Then picture their answer, and picture yourself leaning toward it, curious, the way Montaigne leaned toward whoever contradicted him. The bell holds the time.
The art of conversation. Montaigne's essay on talking, where he calls conversation the mind's most fruitful exercise and welcomes contradiction over flattery. Today's word.
Your line: honest talk. Today, have one honest conversation: say where you differ, kindly, and then really listen to the reply. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: In the essay Of the art of conversing, Montaigne describes welcoming contradiction as a teacher and disliking talk where everyone only agrees; readers often take it as a guide to disagreeing well.

original.note: Montaigne's French title: the art of conferring, of talking things through.

trapdoor: what you thought: the art of conversation is being charming.
what it means: for Montaigne, it's welcoming contradiction, refusing flattery, and caring more for the truth than for winning.
what a scholar hears: the French title uses conférer, to confer or talk things through, and the essay treats talk as an exercise of the mind, not a social grace.
recall: a try, a test, an attempt
